text: What sound do you miss?
evaluation: A warm-up. Listen for whether they go specific (a screen door, a particular voice) or generic. Specificity here predicts depth later.

text: What did you believe about adults that turned out to be wrong?
evaluation: Tells you what disillusionment they've metabolised. Bitter answers are a flag; wry ones a good sign.

text: What time of day do you like yourself most?
evaluation: A surprisingly revealing question. People who can't answer often haven't asked themselves.

text: Where do you go when you want to feel small?
evaluation: Wanting to feel small is a healthy instinct. No answer at all suggests an aversion to humility.

text: What do you reread, and why that one?
evaluation: Rereading is a stronger signal than reading. The 'why' is the real answer.

text: Who do you copy without meaning to?
evaluation: Self-aware people can name the influence without embarrassment. Defensiveness here often masks a parent.

text: What compliment do you remember word for word?
evaluation: What we remember tells us what we were starved for. Note the source, not just the line.

text: What do you own that you would never sell?
evaluation: Tests whether they have a felt relationship to anything physical. 'Nothing' is a real answer worth probing.

text: When were you last surprised by yourself?
evaluation: Indicates whether they're still in motion. People who can't recall are often coasting.

text: What do you find beautiful that most people don't?
evaluation: A taste question. Pretentious answers ring; particular ones land. Listen for whether they sound like they actually look at the world.

text: What do you spend money on to avoid feeling something?
evaluation: Concrete answers (delivery food, subscriptions) signal awareness; vague answers signal denial.

text: Whose approval still matters more than it should?
evaluation: Naming the person is the answer. 'No one' usually means a parent or an ex.

text: What do you keep secret that isn't shameful?
evaluation: Probes their relationship to privacy versus secrecy. People who conflate the two are often hiding things that are shameful.

text: What conversation are you avoiding?
evaluation: If they have one ready, that's good news. If not, the avoidance runs deeper than a single conversation.

text: What version of yourself do you miss?
evaluation: Nostalgia for an earlier self is a normal, useful answer. Contempt for it is information too.

text: What do you envy without admitting it?
evaluation: Naming the envy defuses it. Inability to name any is usually a defense.

text: When were you last bored, and what did it tell you?
evaluation: Boredom is data. Listen for whether they treat it as a signal or a failure to be optimised away.

text: What do you do that you learned from someone you no longer respect?
evaluation: A maturity test. Can they hold the contradiction that something useful came from someone flawed?

text: What part of your day, every day, are you grateful for?
evaluation: Vague gratitude is suspicious. A specific moment — the first coffee, the walk back — is the real signal.

text: What do you want to be asked that no one asks?
evaluation: Doubles as a meta question — gives them a chance to redirect the whole conversation. Take it seriously.

text: What do you find easy that most people find hard?
evaluation: Self-knowledge of strengths without bragging is rare. False modesty is its own tell.

text: What do you find hard that most people find easy?
evaluation: Counterpart to dr021. People who can answer both are usually the ones worth knowing.

text: When did you last cry, and was it a relief?
evaluation: Whether they answer at all is the first signal. The 'relief' part separates suppression from release.

text: What do you do with anger?
evaluation: Listen for: somatic awareness, an actual verb, and whether the strategy seems to work. 'I don't get angry' is the worst answer.

text: What in your life is loud right now? What is quiet?
evaluation: A check-in question disguised as poetry. Useful as a session opener.

text: Who knew you when you were at your worst, and what did they do?
evaluation: Identifies who has standing. Inability to name anyone is a quiet but serious signal.

text: What do you do that you are pretty sure is harmless, but might not be?
evaluation: Tests willingness to inspect their own blind spots. Defensiveness here is the answer.

text: What did your parents get right about you that you only recently saw?
evaluation: A reconciliation question. Tonal — listen for whether the answer comes with warmth or grievance.

text: What did your parents get wrong about you that they still believe?
evaluation: Counterpart. The pair together gives you a map of how they see their family of origin.

text: What do you do when you don't know what to do?
evaluation: A coping-strategy question. Listen for paralysis vs. distraction vs. action vs. asking. All are valid; none can be 'I always know'.

text: What is the kindest thing a stranger has done for you?
evaluation: Whether they have one ready tells you whether they notice.

text: What is the kindest thing you have done for a stranger?
evaluation: If they brag, dock the answer. If they downplay, raise it.

text: What habit are you proud of that took years?
evaluation: Patience is rare. The longer the timeline, the more the answer is worth.

text: What habit are you ashamed of that you haven't broken?
evaluation: Honesty here matters more than the habit itself.

text: Whose life would you swap for, just for a week?
evaluation: A wish question. Tells you what they think they're missing.

text: What part of growing up do you wish had taken longer?
evaluation: Reveals their relationship to their own past — wistful, relieved, indifferent, angry.

text: What do you find romantic that isn't usually called that?
evaluation: Their definition of romance is more useful than their definition of love.

text: What do you do on a free Sunday with no plans?
evaluation: Defaults reveal more than ambitions. The honest answer is rarely the impressive one.

text: What in your home would tell a stranger the most about you?
evaluation: Visual specificity is the test. 'My books' is a non-answer.

text: What do you look forward to that you used to dread?
evaluation: Indicates capacity for change in taste — a proxy for openness.

text: What do you do for people you love that you don't tell them about?
evaluation: If they can name something specific without performing it, that's the signal.

text: When were you wrong about a person and it cost you?
evaluation: Looks for accountability rather than victimhood. Watch the pronouns.

text: When were you wrong about a person, in their favour?
evaluation: The reverse. Generosity in revising upward is rarer than in revising downward.

text: What kind of attention makes you uncomfortable?
evaluation: Useful for understanding what they protect, and how.

text: What kind of attention do you secretly want more of?
evaluation: Counterpart to dr044. Together they map their relationship to being seen.

text: What do you do when someone you love is in pain?
evaluation: Listen for whether they fix, hold, distract, or vanish. None is wrong; mismatch with their partner's need is the issue.

text: What does being loved well feel like, in your body?
evaluation: The somatic frame is intentional. People who can't locate it physically often can't recognise it.

text: What does being loved badly feel like, in your body?
evaluation: Same, in the negative. Pairs with dr047 to reveal pattern recognition.

text: How do you know when you trust someone?
evaluation: Tests whether trust is a feeling, a track record, or a decision for them.

text: How do you know when trust is gone?
evaluation: The exit signs matter as much as the entry signs. Vague answers here often precede repeated heartbreak.

text: What kind of fight do you have over and over?
evaluation: Pattern recognition is the goal. 'I don't fight' is a flag, not a virtue.

text: What do you do after a fight that helps?
evaluation: Repair matters more than fighting style. Listen for a real practice, not a theory.

text: When have you stayed too long?
evaluation: A scar question. Most adults have one. Refusal to name one is itself a pattern.

text: When have you left too soon?
evaluation: Counterpart. Asking both prevents either being weaponised.

text: What do you want from a partner that no one has given you?
evaluation: Distinguish a real unmet need from a fantasy. Specificity again is the test.

text: What have you given a partner that you've never been thanked for?
evaluation: If it sounds rehearsed, it is. Watch tone — bitterness vs. resignation vs. acceptance.

text: What do you want for yourself that has nothing to do with anyone else?
evaluation: Tests whether their wants are ever solo. People entirely defined by others struggle here.

text: What is the lie you tell yourself most often?
evaluation: If they laugh and answer, that's a good sign. If they go silent and then deflect, the lie is closer to the surface than they like.

text: Whose forgiveness do you want and won't ask for?
evaluation: A heavy one — handle in a quieter part of the session.

text: Whose forgiveness has been offered that you haven't accepted?
evaluation: Some people refuse forgiveness because guilt is the only contact left. Worth probing gently.

text: What do you do when someone disappoints you?
evaluation: Listen for whether they say something or stew. Stewing in silence predicts later collapse.

text: What do you do when you disappoint someone?
evaluation: Apology, defensiveness, distance, repair — each has a different cost.

text: What is one thing you've never said out loud?
evaluation: Not a demand to say it. The category they choose tells you the shape.

text: What do you wish your younger self had known, that you wouldn't have believed?
evaluation: The 'wouldn't have believed' part forces them past clichés.

text: What did you survive that you don't talk about?
evaluation: Heavy. Only ask in the right setting. 'Nothing' is a complete answer; respect it.

text: What do you protect, even when no one's looking?
evaluation: Names a value through action rather than statement.

text: What do you think people get wrong about love?
evaluation: Their thesis on love is usually about the love they wish they'd received.

text: What do you do to keep a friendship alive over distance?
evaluation: Real practices are short and consistent. Grand answers here usually mean inconsistent practice.

text: Who could you call right now, at any hour, with bad news?
evaluation: Count the names. Three is healthy. Zero is a quiet emergency.

text: Who would call you, at any hour, with bad news?
evaluation: The reverse matters as much. Asymmetry between dr069 and dr070 is information.

text: What did you used to want that you no longer want?
evaluation: Outgrown desires reveal growth. Inability to name any suggests stalled motion.

text: What do you want now that you suspect you'll outgrow?
evaluation: Self-prediction is hard. The willingness to try is the answer.

text: What part of your body has changed your mind about itself?
evaluation: Especially powerful with people who've made peace with something they once hated.

text: What do you do for pleasure that has no audience?
evaluation: Solo pleasure with no documentation suggests a self that exists for itself.

text: What is the most useful thing a stranger has ever said to you?
evaluation: Tests whether they take counsel from outside their circle.

text: What do you do when you're attracted to someone you shouldn't act on?
evaluation: Sit with their answer. The categories: notice and pass, suppress and resent, indulge in fantasy, act and rationalise.

text: What do you find sexy that has nothing to do with looks?
evaluation: Specificity again separates real desire from script.

text: What do you wish were easier to talk about with a partner?
evaluation: What they name is what they avoid. Useful for setting future agendas.

text: How do you tell a partner no?
evaluation: If they have a sentence, ask them to say it. If they don't, that's the work.

text: How do you tell a partner yes when it costs you?
evaluation: Generosity that comes with resentment isn't generosity. Listen for whether the cost is acknowledged or hidden.

text: What did you learn about love from how your parents loved each other?
evaluation: The lesson is rarely the one the parents intended. Inheritance is the question, not approval.

text: What did you learn about love from how your parents loved you?
evaluation: Companion to dr081. Together they form an attachment-style sketch.

text: What do you do that your parents would not understand?
evaluation: A separation question. Healthy adults can usually answer; enmeshed ones cannot.

text: What do you carry from your parents that you wish you didn't?
evaluation: Watch for absence of bitterness alongside the clarity. Both are signs of work done.

text: What do you carry from your parents that you're glad to?
evaluation: Always pair with dr084 to keep the picture honest.

text: What do you do to keep yourself company?
evaluation: Not loneliness. Solitude. The phrasing matters.

text: Where in the world do you feel most yourself?
evaluation: Place attachment is information. The 'why' is more interesting than the where.

text: Where in the world do you feel least yourself?
evaluation: Counterpart to dr087. Together they reveal the conditions of the self.

text: What do you laugh at when no one is around?
evaluation: Private humour is the truest. Public humour is a costume.

text: What can't you take seriously, no matter how hard you try?
evaluation: Reveals where their irreverence lives. Helpful to know early.

text: What in your life right now is provisional?
evaluation: Most lives have something held loosely. People who say 'nothing' are often more committed than they realise — or more stuck.

text: What in your life right now is permanent?
evaluation: Their definition of permanent is the answer.

text: What was the last thing you changed your mind about?
evaluation: Recency matters. If the last revision was years ago, that's a flag.

text: What is one thing you believe that most of your friends don't?
evaluation: Tests independence of thought without veering into contrarianism.

text: What in this reflection so far has surprised you?
evaluation: Mid-session check-in. Surfaces what you are actually tracking.

text: What have you not been asked, lately, that you wished you had been?
evaluation: A trust question with yourself. The answer is often the next conversation you owe someone.

text: What would you want to be remembered for, by people who know you well?
evaluation: Note the qualifier 'by people who know you well' — it filters out legacy fantasy.

text: What would you want to be remembered for, by people who barely knew you?
evaluation: Together with dr097, separates self-image from social-image.

text: What would you do tomorrow if you knew it would be your only ordinary day for a long time?
evaluation: The word 'ordinary' is doing the work. Watch for whether they reach for grandeur or for the small things.

text: What is one thing about yourself you would only share if someone asked?
evaluation: A closing-friendly question. Surfaces what matters to you about being asked at all.
